lesson.title: Putting the Mean Value Theorem to Work
lesson.summary: The Mean Value Theorem is not just an existence statement to verify on toy examples; it is a working tool for proving that functions with zero derivative are constant, and for pinning down tight numerical bounds on quantities like square roots without a calculator.
lesson.body:
One of the most important uses of the Mean Value Theorem is proving a fact that feels almost too obvious to need a proof: if f'(x) = 0 for every x in some interval, then f is constant on that interval. Here is why the theorem is exactly what makes that rigorous. Pick any two points a and b in the interval, with a less than b. Since f is differentiable everywhere on the interval, its derivative is 0 there, which certainly exists, it is also continuous there, so the Mean Value Theorem applies on [a,b]. It guarantees some c in (a,b) with f'(c) = [f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a). But f'(c) = 0 everywhere by assumption, so [f(b)-f(a)]/(b-a) = 0, which forces f(b) - f(a) = 0, meaning f(b) = f(a). Since a and b were any two points in the interval, every pair of function values is equal, which is exactly what it means for f to be constant. This single argument is the foundation for why two functions with the same derivative everywhere must differ by a constant, a fact used constantly when working with antiderivatives.

The Mean Value Theorem is also a practical tool for bounding hard to compute quantities. Estimate sqrt(101) without a calculator using f(x) = sqrt(x) on the interval [100, 101]. This f is continuous and differentiable on the relevant interval, certainly for x greater than 0, so the theorem guarantees some c strictly between 100 and 101 with f'(c) = [f(101) - f(100)] / (101 - 100) = [sqrt(101) - 10] / 1 = sqrt(101) - 10, since sqrt(100) = 10 exactly. The derivative is f'(x) = 1/(2 sqrt(x)). Now use a bound on c that does not require already knowing sqrt(101): since 100 is less than c, which is less than 101, which is less than 121, and square root is increasing, 10 is less than sqrt(c), which is less than 11. That gives 1/22 less than 1/(2 sqrt(c)) less than 1/20, or roughly 0.0455 less than f'(c) less than 0.05. Since f'(c) equals sqrt(101) - 10, this means 0.0455 is less than sqrt(101) - 10, which is less than 0.05, so 10.0455 is less than sqrt(101), which is less than 10.05. The true value of sqrt(101) is approximately 10.0499, comfortably inside that window, confirming the bound is both valid and reasonably tight, all without ever computing a square root directly.

Both applications follow the same template: use the Mean Value Theorem to replace a statement about the difference in function values, f(b) - f(a), with a statement about a derivative at some unknown but existing point c, and then use whatever is known or can be bounded about that derivative to conclude something about the original difference. This is a genuinely different way of reasoning than direct computation, and it is often the only practical route when a function's exact values are hard to pin down but its rate of change is easy to control.

These two applications, proving constancy from a zero derivative and bounding function values using bounds on the derivative, are representative of how the theorem gets used throughout calculus: not to compute c precisely, but to guarantee c exists and then squeeze useful information out of that guarantee.
